pos: n. (want of knowledge; rendering Greek agnoia)
etymology: From Latin ignorare, not to know. Scripture treats ignorance as real, as culpable, and as no longer excusable once the gospel has been preached.
biblical_def: Ignorance is want of knowledge. The law made provision for sins committed in it, requiring a sacrifice still (Lev 4:2). Christ prays over His executioners, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luk 23:34), and Peter grants the same of the crowd: “I wot that through ignorance ye did it” (Act 3:17). Paul says God “winked at” the times of ignorance “but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ignorance as want of knowledge or instruction; unacquaintance with any thing; and unenlightened state of the mind.
webster_full: IGNORANCE, n. Want of knowledge or instruction; unacquaintance with any thing.
2. In theology, ignorance is the want of knowledge of God and of his will.
scriptures: And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers.

Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If a soul shall sin through ignorance against any of the commandments of the LORD concerning things which ought not to be done, and shall do against any of them:
corruption_summary: Ignorance is claimed as an exemption, and Scripture treats it as a mercy that shortens the sentence rather than an acquittal that cancels it.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 4 settles the question early: a sin committed in ignorance is still a sin requiring atonement. The offender is guilty, and when the matter comes to his knowledge he must bring an offering. That is a hard doctrine and a merciful one — hard, because sincerity does not sterilize an act; merciful, because provision is made for precisely the offences a man could not have avoided knowing about.

Acts 17:30 marks the hinge of history: the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent. Ignorance had bought time; the resurrection ended the window. Paul says it to Athenians who prided themselves on knowledge, and the effect is to remove the last respectable place to stand — nobody in earshot of the gospel is ignorant in the sense that once excused.
roots_summary: Greek agnoia (G52), ignorance; agnoeo (G50), not to know; Hebrew shegagah (H7684), an inadvertent sin.
roots_lines: Greek agnoia (G52) — ignorance; Acts 3:17, 17:30, Ephesians 4:18, 1 Peter 1:14.
Hebrew shegagah (H7684) — error, sin of ignorance; Leviticus 4:2, 22, Numbers 15:24-29.
usage: “The times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth… repent” — the window closed.
“They know not what they do” — ignorance pleaded from the cross.
“If a soul shall sin through ignorance” — still a sin, and still provided for.

pos: n. (the mind's devising; rendering Hebrew yetser, Greek dialogismos)
etymology: From Latin imaginari, to picture. The Hebrew yetser means what is formed or framed — imagination as a workshop, not a daydream.
biblical_def: Imagination is the mind's devising. Genesis gives the flood's cause in these terms: “God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Gen 6:5), and repeats it after the flood as a permanent diagnosis (Gen 8:21). Paul's warfare is aimed there: “casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God” (2Co 10:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imagination as the power or faculty of the mind by which it conceives and forms ideas of things; and conceit, an unsolid or fanciful opinion.
webster_full: IMAGINATION, n. The power or faculty of the mind by which it conceives and forms ideas of things communicated to it by the organs of sense.
2. Conception; image in the mind; idea.
3. Contrivance; scheme formed in the mind; device.
4. Conceit; an unsolid or fanciful opinion.
scriptures: And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.

And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done. a
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: The inner life is treated as private and therefore harmless, and Genesis locates the cause of the flood in what men were forming in their hearts.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 6:5 is the most sweeping verdict in Scripture on human nature, and every word narrows it further: every imagination, of the thoughts, of his heart, was only evil, continually. Not most, not sometimes. The Hebrew yetser is a potter's word — what is shaped or framed — so the charge concerns the workshop where intentions are made, before anything is done. That is why the flood is described as grief in God rather than mere anger.

2 Corinthians 10 gives the battlefield and the weapons. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds; casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ. The imagination is a fortified position, and Paul's siege equipment is spiritual because the walls are.
roots_summary: Hebrew yetser (H3336), a thing framed, purpose, imagination — from yatsar, to form as a potter; Greek logismos (G3053), a reasoning.
roots_lines: Hebrew yetser (H3336) — imagination, framing, purpose; Genesis 6:5, 8:21, 1 Chronicles 29:18.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, fashion; the potter's verb behind it.
Greek logismos (G3053) — reasoning, imagination; 2 Corinthians 10:5, Romans 2:15.
usage: “Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” — the workshop indicted.
“Casting down imaginations” — a fortified position under siege.
“Bringing into captivity every thought” — the aim of the campaign.

pos: n. (decay, moral rot; rendering Hebrew shachath, Greek phthora)
etymology: From Latin corrumpere, to break utterly. Corruption in Scripture is decay — and its defeat is stated in the language of a body that did not rot.
biblical_def: Corruption is decay. David's psalm, quoted at Pentecost, promises escape from it: “thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Psa 16:10) — and Peter presses the point that David died and saw corruption, so the psalm speaks of another (Act 2:31). Paul makes it the resurrection's central contrast: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption” (1Co 15:42), and Peter says we are made partakers of the divine nature, “having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust” (2Pe 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corruption as the act of corrupting, or state of being corrupt; putrefaction; and depravity, wickedness, perversion of principles.
webster_full: CORRUPTION, n. The act of corrupting, or state of being corrupt or putrid; the destruction of the natural form of bodies.
2. Depravity; wickedness; perversion or deterioration of moral principles.
3. Bribery.
scriptures: For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.
So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
corruption_summary: Decay is treated as a natural process to be delayed, and Scripture treats it as an enemy already defeated in one particular body.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's Pentecost argument turns on a grave. David spoke of not seeing corruption, but David is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day. Therefore the psalm was not about him. He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption. The whole sermon rests on the observable fact that one tomb in Jerusalem was empty and the other was not.

1 Corinthians 15:42 extends it to everyone in Christ: it is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption. Paul is describing burial as sowing, which reframes a grave as a planting rather than a disposal. The corruption is real — he does not pretend otherwise — and it is the condition from which something better is raised.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath (H7845), a pit, decay; Greek phthora (G5356), decay, ruin; diaphthora (G1312), thorough decay — the word in Acts 2:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7845) — pit, corruption; Psalm 16:10, Job 17:14.
Greek diaphthora (G1312) — corruption, decay; Acts 2:27, 31, 13:34-37.
Greek aphtharsia (G861) — incorruption; 1 Corinthians 15:42, 50, 53.
usage: “Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” — the psalm Peter pressed.
“It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption” — a grave as a planting.
“Having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust” — moral decay named.

pos: n. (waiting, hope; rendering Hebrew tiqvah, Greek apokaradokia)
etymology: From Latin expectare, to look out for. The Greek word Paul uses means to watch with the head stretched forward — expectation with a posture.
biblical_def: Expectation is forward-looking waiting. The psalmist locates his: “My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him” (Psa 62:5). Proverbs contrasts two futures: “the expectation of the wicked shall perish” (Pro 10:28), and “there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off” (Pro 23:18). Paul writes of “the earnest expectation of the creature… waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God” (Rom 8:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expectation as the act of expecting; the state of waiting for an event; and the prospect of good to come.
webster_full: EXPECTATION, n. The act of expecting or looking forward to a future event with at least some reason to believe the event will happen.
2. The state of waiting for an event to take place.
3. Prospect of good to come.
scriptures: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
The hope of the righteous shall be gladness: but the expectation of the wicked shall perish.
For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.
For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off.
corruption_summary: Disappointment is treated as evidence that hope was foolish, and the psalmist's remedy is not lower expectation but a different object for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 62:5 does not counsel expecting less; it relocates the expectation: my soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him. The word only is doing the work. A soul with several sources of expectation is a soul with several possible disappointments, and the psalm's answer to a crumbling world — men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie — is to narrow the account to one Payer.

Romans 8:19 gives expectation a cosmic scale and a strange subject: the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. Creation itself is craning forward. The Greek pictures a watcher with the head thrust out, and what it is watching for is not the end of the world but the revealing of God's children — because the deliverance of the one runs through the glorification of the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew tiqvah (H8615), hope, expectation — the same word as Rahab's cord; Greek apokaradokia (G603), watching with outstretched head.
roots_lines: Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — hope, expectation, cord; Proverbs 10:28, 23:18, Jeremiah 29:11.
Greek apokaradokia (G603) — earnest expectation; Romans 8:19, Philippians 1:20.
Hebrew tochelet (H8431) — expectation; Proverbs 13:12, hope deferred maketh the heart sick.
usage: “My expectation is from him” — one account, one Payer.
“The earnest expectation of the creature” — creation craning forward.
“Thine expectation shall not be cut off” — the promise to the God-fearer.

pos: n. (freedom from guilt; rendering Hebrew niqqayon, Aramaic zaku)
etymology: From Latin innocens, not harming. Innocency is the older form of innocence, and the KJV uses it of both moral cleanness and legal acquittal.
biblical_def: Innocency is freedom from guilt. Daniel explains his survival among the lions: “My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt” (Dan 6:22). The psalmist washes his hands in innocency and compasses the altar (Psa 26:6), and Hosea's charge against Israel is that they have not attained it (Hos 8:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines innocence or innocency as freedom from guilt or the imputation of guilt; harmlessness; innoxiousness; and simplicity of heart.
webster_full: INNOCENCE, INNOCENCY, n. Properly, freedom from any quality that can injure; innoxiousness; harmlessness.
2. In a moral sense, freedom from crime, sin or guilt.
3. Freedom from guilt in a particular act.
scriptures: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt.
I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD:
Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off; mine anger is kindled against them: how long will it be ere they attain to innocency?

Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God.
corruption_summary: Vindication is expected to arrive before the ordeal, and Daniel's innocency was declared by God at dawn, after a night with the lions.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 6:22 puts the innocency in the right court. Before him innocency was found in me — God's verdict first, and only then, and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt. Daniel had been condemned by a legally valid decree, thrown to real lions, and sealed in with the king's own signet. The innocence did not prevent the pit; it determined what happened inside it. Verse 23 adds the reason no hurt was found: because he believed in his God.

Psalm 26:6 shows the practice attached: I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD. The washing is a preparation for worship, not a claim to sinlessness — the same psalm asks God to examine and prove him. Approaching the altar with clean hands is a discipline of self-examination, and Pilate's later hand-washing is its counterfeit: the same gesture with the opposite intention.
roots_summary: Hebrew niqqayon (H5356), cleanness, innocency; Aramaic zaku (H2118), innocency, in Daniel 6:22.
roots_lines: Aramaic zaku (H2118) — innocence; only Daniel 6:22.
Hebrew niqqayon (H5356) — cleanness, innocency; Psalm 26:6, 73:13, Genesis 20:5.
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — innocent, clean; Psalm 24:4, he that hath clean hands.
usage: “Before him innocency was found in me” — the verdict that mattered first.
“I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar” — preparation for worship.
“Because he believed in his God” — why no hurt was found.

pos: n. (God's coming in mercy or judgment; rendering Hebrew pequddah, Greek episkope)
etymology: From Latin visitare, to go to see. A visitation is God arriving — and Scripture uses the same word for the day of reckoning and the day of mercy.
biblical_def: A visitation is God's coming. Christ weeps over Jerusalem and names the reason for its ruin: “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luk 19:44). Peter urges good conduct among the Gentiles “that… they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation” (1Pe 2:12). Jeremiah warns of a visitation in judgment (Jer 8:12), and Job asks what he shall answer when God visits (Job 31:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines visitation as the act of visiting; and in a scriptural sense, a coming of God, either in mercy or in judgment, for the purpose of inspection or trial.
webster_full: VISITATION, n. The act of visiting.
2. Object of visit.
3. In a scriptural sense, special dispensation of divine favor or wrath; a coming of God to reward or punish.
scriptures: And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore shall they fall among them that fall: in the time of their visitation they shall be cast down, saith the LORD.
What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?
corruption_summary: God's coming is expected to be unmistakable, and Christ wept over a city that missed His because it did not look like what they were watching for.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 19:41-44 is the only place the Gospels record Christ weeping over a place rather than a person, and the diagnosis is one clause long: because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation. Jerusalem was not irreligious, inattentive, or uninformed; it was watching for a different kind of arrival. He came riding a foal, and the city that had prophets, scriptures, and a temple failed to recognize the visit it had been waiting centuries for.

Peter's use runs forward rather than back. Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation. The Christian's ordinary conduct is being stored as evidence for a day when God comes to a watching neighbour — which makes an unremarkable, honest life a form of advance work.
roots_summary: Hebrew pequddah (H6486), visitation, oversight, mustering; Greek episkope (G1984), a visitation or overseership — the same root as bishop.
roots_lines: Hebrew pequddah (H6486) — visitation, oversight; Jeremiah 8:12, 10:15, Isaiah 10:3.
Greek episkope (G1984) — visitation, office of oversight; Luke 19:44, 1 Peter 2:12, 1 Timothy 3:1.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, look upon; Luke 1:68, he hath visited and redeemed his people.
usage: “Thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” — the clause He wept over.
“Glorify God in the day of visitation” — ordinary conduct as advance work.
“What then shall I do when God riseth up?” — Job's question.

pos: n. (living without regard to God; rendering Greek asebeia)
etymology: Un with godliness. The Greek asebeia means irreverence — not primarily immorality but a failure to render God His due.
biblical_def: Ungodliness is disregard of God. Paul names it as the first object of wrath: “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom 1:18) — ungodliness first, unrighteousness following from it. Grace teaches its denial: “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly” (Tit 2:12). And Christ died for the ungodly (Rom 5:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ungodliness as impiety; wickedness; neglect of God and his commands.
webster_full: UNGODLINESS, n. Impiety; wickedness; neglect of God and of his commands.
UNGODLY, a. Wicked; impious; neglecting the fear and worship of God, or violating his commands.
scriptures: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness;
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.

To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.
corruption_summary: Sin is catalogued as behaviour, and Paul puts ungodliness first — the failure to honour God as God, from which the behaviour follows.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1 orders the indictment deliberately: ungodliness and unrighteousness. Paul then traces the sequence — when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations. The moral collapse catalogued later in the chapter is presented as consequence, not cause. That order matters pastorally, because a church addressing only the behaviour is treating symptoms and leaving the disease.

Titus 2:12 shows grace doing what law could not: the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world. Grace is a teacher with a curriculum, and its first lesson is denial. Anyone who has understood grace as permission has not attended the class Paul describes.
roots_summary: Greek asebeia (G763), impiety, ungodliness; asebes (G765), ungodly — the ones for whom Christ died in Romans 5:6.
roots_lines: Greek asebeia (G763) — ungodliness; Romans 1:18, Titus 2:12, Jude 15, 18.
Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly; Romans 4:5, 5:6, 1 Peter 4:18, 2 Peter 2:5.
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness; the positive Paul sets against it.
usage: “Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness” — the order is the diagnosis.
“Denying ungodliness and worldly lusts” — grace as a teacher.
“Christ died for the ungodly” — the class He came for.

pos: n. (public standing; rendering Greek doxa and timios)
etymology: From Latin reputare, to reckon. A reputation is what others reckon a person to be — and Philippians 2 describes Christ setting His aside.
biblical_def: Reputation is public standing. Philippians describes Christ's treatment of His own: “who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant” (Php 2:6–7). Paul mentions those “who seemed to be somewhat” at Jerusalem and adds that God accepteth no man's person (Gal 2:6). Ecclesiastes warns that “dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour” (Ecc 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reputation as good name; the credit, honor or character which is derived from a favorable public opinion or esteem.
webster_full: REPUTATION, n. Good name; the credit, honor or character which is derived from a favorable public opinion or esteem.
2. Character by report; in a good or bad sense.
3. Fame; celebrity.
scriptures: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.
But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
corruption_summary: Reputation is built and defended as the ministry's real asset, and Philippians 2 makes emptying it the pattern every Christian is commanded to have.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 2:5 attaches a command to the passage: let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. What follows is not primarily a doctrinal statement to admire but a pattern to copy — He made himself of no reputation. The Greek is that He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant. Whatever else Christian humility means, it includes the willing surrender of standing one is genuinely entitled to.

Ecclesiastes 10:1 is the sober counterweight for anyone who has a reputation to lose. Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour. The proportions are cruel and accurate: a small quantity of folly ruins a large quantity of good, and the higher the reputation the smaller the fly needs to be.
roots_summary: Greek kenoo (G2758), to empty — made himself of no reputation; doxa (G1391), glory or repute; dokeo (G1380), to seem, in Galatians 2:6.
roots_lines: Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, make of no reputation; Philippians 2:7.
Greek dokeo (G1380) — to seem, be of repute; Galatians 2:2, 6, 9.
Greek morphe (G3444) — form; the form of God and the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7.
usage: “Made himself of no reputation” — standing genuinely owed, willingly surrendered.
“Let this mind be in you” — the passage is a command before it is a doctrine.
“Dead flies cause the ointment… to send forth a stinking savour” — small folly, large loss.

pos: n. (completeness, maturity; rendering Greek teleiotes)
etymology: From Latin perficere, to finish. The Greek teleios means brought to its end or purpose — perfection as completeness rather than flawlessness.
biblical_def: Perfection is completeness. Hebrews urges progress: “leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection” (Heb 6:1). Paul disclaims arrival while pressing on: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after… I press toward the mark” (Php 3:12,14). Colossians names love as the binding term: “charity, which is the bond of perfectness” (Col 3:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perfection as the state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; and physical perfection, that state in which natural powers and faculties are entire.
webster_full: PERFECTION, n. The state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting.
2. Physical perfection, is when a natural object has all its powers, faculties or qualities entire and in full operation.
3. Moral perfection, is the complete possession of all moral excellence.
scriptures: Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
corruption_summary: Perfection is read as flawlessness and therefore either claimed dishonestly or abandoned entirely, when the New Testament means completeness — a thing brought to its purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 3 holds the two halves together in a way most teaching separates. Paul denies arrival plainly — not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect — and in the same breath commits to pursuit: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. Honest about the distance, relentless about the direction. Both claiming perfection and giving up on it fail this test.

Hebrews 6:1 uses the word for maturity and treats staying at the foundations as a problem. Leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation. Foundations are essential and are laid once. A congregation that hears only conversion preaching for twenty years is not being kept safe; it is being kept unfinished.
roots_summary: Greek teleios (G5046), complete, mature; teleiotes (G5047), completeness; teleioo (G5048), to bring to an end — the verb of it is finished.
roots_lines: Greek teleios (G5046) — perfect, complete, mature; Matthew 5:48, 1 Corinthians 14:20, be men.
Greek teleiotes (G5047) — perfection; Hebrews 6:1, Colossians 3:14.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to complete, finish; Hebrews 10:14, he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
usage: “Let us go on unto perfection” — foundations laid once, not repeatedly.
“Not as though I had already attained” — honest distance, relentless direction.
“Charity, which is the bond of perfectness” — love holds completeness together.

pos: n. (success, flourishing; rendering Hebrew shalvah and tsalach)
etymology: From Latin prosperare, to cause to succeed. Scripture treats prosperity as a real blessing and a serious hazard, often in the same passage.
biblical_def: Prosperity is flourishing. Ecclesiastes sets it opposite adversity as equally appointed: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider” (Ecc 7:14). The psalmist confesses envying the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary (Psa 73:3,17). Solomon's own dedication asks for wisdom rather than riches, and prosperity followed unasked (1Ki 3:11–13); and David warns, “in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved” (Psa 30:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prosperity as advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; success; attainment of the object desired.
webster_full: PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; success; attainment of the object desired.
scriptures: In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.
For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
And in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved.
Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is read as proof of God's approval, and Psalm 73 records a believer nearly losing his footing over how well the wicked were doing.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 73 is the most honest chapter in Scripture about envy. My feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist catalogues their ease, their health, their freedom from trouble, and admits the conclusion he drew: verily I have cleansed my heart in vain. What changed was not his circumstances but his vantage point — until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.

David's line in Psalm 30:6 is the shortest diagnosis of prosperity's hazard: in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved. Nothing sinful is described. The danger is a sentence a comfortable man says to himself, and the next verse records what it took to correct it: thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalvah (H7962), ease, prosperity; tsalach (H6743), to prosper or succeed; shalom (H7965), peace, welfare.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalvah (H7962) — ease, prosperity; Psalm 73:3, Proverbs 1:32, the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper; Genesis 39:2, Joshua 1:8, Psalm 1:3.
Hebrew tob (H2896) — good; Ecclesiastes 7:14, the day of prosperity.
usage: “I was envious… when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” — a believer nearly slipping.
“Until I went into the sanctuary of God” — the vantage point that changed.
“In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved” — the sentence comfort teaches.

pos: n. (a league or alliance; rendering Hebrew qesher and berith)
etymology: From Latin confoederare, to league together. Scripture's confederacies are usually alliances formed by fear against God's people, or by His people instead of trusting Him.
biblical_def: A confederacy is an alliance. Isaiah is warned not to join the national panic: “Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear” (Isa 8:12–13). Psalm 83 lists the nations that “are confederate against thee” (Psa 83:5), and Obadiah rebukes the men of Edom's confederacy (Oba 7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confederacy as a league, or covenant; a contract between two or more persons, bodies of men or states, combined in support of each other.
webster_full: CONFEDERACY, n. A league, or covenant; a contract between two or more persons, bodies of men or states, combined in support of each other, in some act or enterprise; mutual engagement; federal compact.
2. The persons, states or nations united by a league.
scriptures: Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid.
Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.
For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee:

All the men of thy confederacy have brought thee even to the border: the men that were at peace with thee have deceived thee, and prevailed against thee; they that eat thy bread have laid a wound under thee: there is none understanding in him.
corruption_summary: Fear looks for allies, and Isaiah was told not even to use the word the whole nation was using — because shared alarm becomes its own authority.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 8:12 forbids a vocabulary before it forbids an action: say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy. The nation had a word for the crisis, and repeating it kept the panic circulating. God's instruction is to stop saying what everyone is saying, and the replacement is given in the next verse: sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. One fear displaces the others.

The promise attached is double-edged: he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel. The same God is refuge or obstacle depending on whether He is feared rightly. A church swept into whatever alarm the culture is currently circulating has, in Isaiah's terms, chosen the wrong fear — and will find the rock where it hoped for the sanctuary.
roots_summary: Hebrew qesher (H7195), a conspiracy or confederacy; berith (H1285), covenant — Psalm 83:5, they have made a covenant against thee.
roots_lines: Hebrew qesher (H7195) — conspiracy, confederacy; Isaiah 8:12, 2 Kings 11:14.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant, league; Psalm 83:5, Obadiah 7.
Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — sanctuary; Isaiah 8:14, he shall be for a sanctuary.
usage: “Say ye not, A confederacy” — a vocabulary forbidden before an action.
“Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” — one fear displacing the others.
“They are confederate against thee” — the nations in Psalm 83.

pos: n. (purity, freedom from defilement; rendering Hebrew bor and niqqayon)
etymology: From clean, Old English claene. Cleanness in Scripture is both ceremonial and moral, and the prophets keep collapsing the distinction.
biblical_def: Cleanness is freedom from defilement. David describes God's dealing: “The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me” (Psa 18:20). Amos uses it with bitter irony of famine: “I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places: yet have ye not returned unto me” (Amo 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cleanness as freedom from dirt, filth or foreign matter; neatness; purity; and innocence.
webster_full: CLEANNESS, n. Freedom from dirt, filth, or foreign matter; neatness.
2. Purity; innocence; freedom from guilt.
3. Exactness; purity; justness; correctness; used of language.
scriptures: The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me.
And I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.
Therefore hath the LORD recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight.
corruption_summary: Hardship is expected to produce repentance automatically, and Amos records five disasters each followed by the same refrain — yet have ye not returned unto me.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 4 is a grim litany. Famine, drought, blight, locusts, pestilence, and overthrow, each followed by the identical sentence: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD. Cleanness of teeth is Amos's phrase for empty mouths, and the irony is savage — the only cleanness Israel achieved was starvation. The chapter refutes the assumption that suffering reliably produces repentance; it produces repentance only where God grants it.

Psalm 18:20-24 raises a question worth answering honestly. David speaks of being rewarded according to the cleanness of his hands, which sits oddly beside a man who wrote Psalm 51. The psalm is about a specific matter — his conduct toward Saul, where he genuinely kept himself from iniquity. Scripture permits a believer to plead integrity in a particular case without claiming it in general.
roots_summary: Hebrew bor (H1252), cleanness, purity; niqqayon (H5356), cleanness — used both of hands and, ironically, of teeth in Amos.
roots_lines: Hebrew bor (H1252) — cleanness, purity; Psalm 18:20, 24, 2 Samuel 22:21.
Hebrew niqqayon (H5356) — cleanness; Amos 4:6, Psalm 26:6.
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — clean, innocent; Psalm 24:4, he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
usage: “According to the cleanness of my hands” — integrity pleaded in a particular case.
“Cleanness of teeth in all your cities” — Amos's savage irony for famine.
“Yet have ye not returned unto me” — the refrain after every disaster.

pos: n. (awe-inspiring power; rendering Hebrew yare and morah)
etymology: From Latin terrere, to frighten. In older English terrible meant awe-inspiring rather than merely bad, and the KJV uses it of God with no negative sense.
biblical_def: Terribleness is awe-inspiring power. David ascribes it to God: “to make thee a name of greatness and terribleness” (1Ch 17:21). Moses recounts the exodus “by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm, and by great terribleness” (Deu 26:8). Jeremiah says of God, “the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one” (Jer 20:11), and Nehemiah prays to “the great and terrible God” (Neh 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terrible as frightful, adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable; and awful, adapted to impress dread or veneration.
webster_full: TERRIBLE, a. Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.
2. Adapted to impress dread, terror or solemn awe and reverence.
3. Severe; rigid.
scriptures: And the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terribleness, and with signs, and with wonders:
And said, I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments:

But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail: they shall be greatly ashamed; for they shall not prosper: their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten.

And what one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel, whom God went to redeem to be his own people, to make thee a name of greatness and terribleness, by driving out nations from before thy people, whom thou hast redeemed out of Egypt?
corruption_summary: A God who inspires dread is thought incompatible with a God who is loved, and Scripture's saints regularly address Him as great and terrible in the middle of asking for mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 1:5 is a prayer, and its opening address is worth noticing: I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him. Terrible and covenant-keeping in the same sentence, spoken by a man about to ask a favour. The awe is not an obstacle to intimacy; it is what makes the mercy remarkable. Prayer that has lost the first half tends to lose the wonder of the second.

Jeremiah 20:11 shows the doctrine under persecution: but the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble. The prophet had just been in the stocks and was in the middle of the most despairing chapter he wrote. What steadied him was not that God is gentle but that God is formidable — and on his side.
roots_summary: Hebrew yare (H3372), to fear, be awesome; nora, the participle rendered terrible; morah (H4172), terror, awe.
roots_lines: Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, revere; the participle nora, terrible, awesome; Nehemiah 1:5, Psalm 66:5.
Hebrew morah (H4172) — terror, awe; Deuteronomy 26:8, great terribleness.
Hebrew arits (H6184) — mighty, terrible one; Jeremiah 20:11.
usage: “The great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy” — awe inside a prayer for favour.
“By great terribleness” — how the exodus is described.
“The LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one” — what steadied Jeremiah.

pos: n. (health, wholeness; rendering Hebrew methom, Greek holokleria)
etymology: From sound, Old English gesund, healthy. Soundness in Scripture covers bodies, doctrine, and speech — all judged by whether they are whole.
biblical_def: Soundness is wholeness. Isaiah's diagnosis of the nation is medical: “From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores” (Isa 1:6). Peter says of the healed lame man that faith in Christ's name “hath given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all” (Act 3:16). The psalmist confesses, “there is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger” (Psa 38:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soundness as wholeness; a state of being free from disease or defect; firmness; strength; and truth; rectitude; as soundness of doctrine.
webster_full: SOUNDNESS, n. A state of being free from disease or defect; a state of health.
2. Firmness; strength; solidity.
3. Truth; rectitude; firmness; freedom from error or fallacy; orthodoxy; as soundness of faith.
scriptures: From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment.
And his name through faith in his name hath made this man strong, whom ye see and know: yea, the faith which is by him hath given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.
There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin.
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
corruption_summary: Doctrine is judged by whether it is interesting or effective, and Paul's category for it is medical — sound teaching is healthy teaching, and the alternative makes people sick.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's phrase to Titus is sound doctrine, and the adjective is the ordinary Greek word for healthy. Speak thou the things which become sound doctrine. The metaphor governs the whole pastoral vocabulary: false teaching eats as doth a canker, unsound words are a gangrene, and healthy teaching produces a healthy congregation. Whether a doctrine is sound is therefore a question about what it does to the body over years, which is slower and more reliable than asking whether it excites.

Isaiah 1:6 applies the same medical eye to a nation: from the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it. And the next clause is the indictment that stings — they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment. Untreated wounds in a body that had priests, prophets, and a temple. The resources for healing were present and unused.
roots_summary: Hebrew methom (H4974), soundness, a sound spot; Greek holokleria (G3647), perfect soundness; hugiaino (G5198), to be healthy — the root of hygiene.
roots_lines: Hebrew methom (H4974) — soundness; Isaiah 1:6, Psalm 38:3, 7.
Greek holokleria (G3647) — perfect soundness; only Acts 3:16.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy; 1 Timothy 1:10, 2 Timothy 4:3, Titus 2:1.
usage: “There is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises” — a nation examined as a body.
“This perfect soundness in the presence of you all” — healing nobody could dispute.
“The things which become sound doctrine” — healthy teaching for a healthy body.

pos: n. (undivided sincerity; rendering Greek haplotes)
etymology: From single, Latin singulus, one. Singleness is the opposite of duplicity — one motive rather than two running at once.
biblical_def: Singleness is undivided sincerity. Luke describes the first church breaking bread “with gladness and singleness of heart” (Act 2:46). Paul commands servants to obey “in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers” (Eph 6:5–6; Col 3:22). Christ uses the related image: “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” (Mat 6:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines singleness as the state of being one only or separate from all others; and simplicity, sincerity, purity of mind or purpose, freedom from duplicity.
webster_full: SINGLENESS, n. The state of being one only or separate from all others.
2. Simplicity; sincerity; purity of mind or purpose; freedom from duplicity; honest plainness.
scriptures: And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ;
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:
corruption_summary: Mixed motives are accepted as inevitable and therefore never examined, and Christ ties the whole body's light to whether the eye is single.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 6:22-23 sits in the middle of teaching about money, which is not accidental. The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. Immediately after comes no man can serve two masters. A single eye is one that wants one thing; a divided eye admits enough darkness to make the whole system dark, and Christ adds the chilling line — if therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!

Ephesians 6:5 applies it to work, and the phrase not with eyeservice, as menpleasers is uncomfortably precise. Eyeservice is labour calibrated to who is watching. Singleness of heart means the quality of the work does not change when the supervisor leaves, because the actual audience never does.
roots_summary: Greek haplotes (G572), singleness, simplicity, liberality; haplous (G573), single, clear — the single eye of Matthew 6:22.
roots_lines: Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, simplicity; Acts 2:46, Ephesians 6:5, Colossians 3:22, 2 Corinthians 11:3.
Greek haplous (G573) — single, sound; Matthew 6:22, Luke 11:34.
Greek ophthalmodouleia (G3787) — eyeservice; Ephesians 6:6, Colossians 3:22.
usage: “With gladness and singleness of heart” — the first church at table.
“Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers” — work calibrated to no watcher.
“If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” — wanting one thing.

pos: n. (refusal to obey; rendering Greek parakoe)
etymology: Dis with obedience. The Greek parakoe means hearing amiss — disobedience as a failure at the point of listening.
biblical_def: Disobedience is refusal to obey. Paul makes it the hinge of history: “as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). Hebrews warns that every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward (Heb 2:2), and Ephesians speaks of “the children of disobedience” in whom the spirit of the world now works (Eph 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disobedience as neglect or refusal to obey; violation of a command or prohibition.
webster_full: DISOBEDIENCE, n. Neglect or refusal to obey; violation of a command or prohibition; the omission of that which is commanded to be done, or the doing of that which is forbid.
scriptures: For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
For if the word spoken by angels was stedfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward;
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.
corruption_summary: Sin is imagined as a series of independent acts, and Romans 5 presents the race as standing under one man's disobedience until it stands under Another's obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 5:19 is built as a balance, and both halves are equally offensive to modern individualism: as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. If the first clause is rejected as unfair, the second goes with it, since they stand on the same principle of representation. The doctrine that lets Adam's act count against me is the doctrine that lets Christ's act count for me.

The Greek parakoe is a hearing word — hearing beside, hearing amiss. Disobedience begins at the ear before it reaches the hand, which is why Hebrews' warning is framed as how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation. Neglect is not defiance; it is simply not attending, and Scripture treats it as the same road.
roots_summary: Greek parakoe (G3876), a mishearing, disobedience; apeitheia (G543), obstinate unbelief — the children of disobedience.
roots_lines: Greek parakoe (G3876) — disobedience, mishearing; Romans 5:19, 2 Corinthians 10:6, Hebrews 2:2.
Greek apeitheia (G543) — disobedience, unbelief; Ephesians 2:2, 5:6, Colossians 3:6.
Greek hupakoe (G5218) — obedience, hearing under; the positive of Romans 5:19.
usage: “By one man's disobedience many were made sinners” — and the remedy runs the same way.
“The children of disobedience” — a family named by its refusal.
“How shall we escape, if we neglect” — neglect is the same road.

pos: n. (the state of the Gentile; rendering Greek akrobustia)
etymology: Un with circumcision. Paul takes a term of contempt and makes it theologically weightless — and that is the argument.
biblical_def: Uncircumcision named the Gentile condition. Paul empties the category of saving significance: “circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” (1Co 7:19), and again, “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love” (Gal 5:6). Romans presses further: if the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision? (Rom 2:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uncircumcision as want of circumcision; and in Scripture, Gentiles, or those who are not circumcised.
webster_full: UNCIRCUMCISION, n. Want of circumcision.
2. In Scripture, Gentiles; those who are not circumcised.
scriptures: Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.
For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.
Therefore if the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision?
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
corruption_summary: Every generation finds a badge that sorts insiders from outsiders, and Paul's method is not to change the badge but to declare the whole category weightless.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's move in 1 Corinthians 7:19 is more radical than it looks. He does not say uncircumcision is now acceptable; he says circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Both sides of the most fiercely defended boundary in his world are pronounced weightless, and what replaces them is the keeping of the commandments of God. The badge is not swapped for a better badge; the category is dissolved.

Romans 2:29 supplies the positive: he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God. The last clause is the giveaway. Every outward badge exists partly to secure praise of men, and an inward mark cannot serve that purpose — which is precisely why it is the one God uses.
roots_summary: Greek akrobustia (G203), uncircumcision; peritome (G4061), circumcision — Paul sets the pair against faith working by love.
roots_lines: Greek akrobustia (G203) — uncircumcision; Romans 2:25-27, 1 Corinthians 7:19, Galatians 5:6, Colossians 3:11.
Greek peritome (G4061) — circumcision; the counterpart term throughout Paul.
Hebrew mul (H4135) — to circumcise; Deuteronomy 30:6, the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart.
usage: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing” — the category dissolved.
“Faith which worketh by love” — what replaces the badge.
“Whose praise is not of men, but of God” — why the mark is inward.

pos: n. (vehemence, fury; rendering Hebrew charon, Greek thumos)
etymology: From Latin ferus, wild. Fierceness in Scripture belongs to God's anger, to men's, and to the beasts — and the distinctions matter.
biblical_def: Fierceness is vehemence. Scripture speaks of “the fierceness of his anger” repeatedly (Nah 1:6), and Revelation of “the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God” (Rev 19:15). Jacob's dying words condemn it in his sons: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel” (Gen 49:7). Jonah's Nineveh turns from evil that God might “turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not” (Jon 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fierceness as ferocity; savageness; and vehemence, fury, impetuosity.
webster_full: FIERCENESS, n. Ferocity; savageness.
2. Eagerness for blood; fury; as the fierceness of a lion.
3. Quickness to attack; keenness in anger and resentment.
4. Violence; outrageous passion.
5. Vehemence; fury; impetuosity; as the fierceness of a tempest.
scriptures: Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him.
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?

And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.
corruption_summary: Human fierceness is excused as passion for a cause, and Jacob's deathbed verdict on Simeon and Levi curses the anger while blessing the men.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 49:7 is a careful piece of moral surgery. Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. Jacob does not curse Simeon and Levi; he curses the thing in them, and then scatters them in Israel. Their cause at Shechem had genuine grievance behind it — their sister had been violated — and the fierceness of the response is condemned anyway. A just cause does not sanctify an unjust ferocity.

Jonah 3:9 shows the response fierceness in God is designed to provoke: who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not? A pagan king reasoned correctly that announced wrath was an invitation to repent, and Nahum 1:6 asks the question that makes the invitation urgent — who can stand before his indignation? Nobody, which is the point of the warning.
roots_summary: Hebrew charon (H2740), burning anger; af (H639), nostril, anger; Greek thumos (G2372), passionate heat.
roots_lines: Hebrew charon (H2740) — burning, fierce anger; Jonah 3:9, Nahum 1:6, Exodus 32:12.
Hebrew az (H5794) — strong, fierce; Genesis 49:7, cursed be their anger, for it was fierce.
Greek thumos (G2372) — fierceness, wrath; Revelation 16:19, 19:15.
usage: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce” — the cause was just, the fury was not.
“Turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not” — a pagan reasoning rightly.
“Who can stand before his indignation?” — the question that makes warning urgent.

pos: n. (condition or rank; rendering Greek tapeinosis and arche)
etymology: From Latin status, a standing. Estate in the KJV means condition or station rather than property, and Mary's song turns on it.
biblical_def: An estate is a condition or station. Mary's Magnificat begins there: “he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luk 1:48). Jude speaks of angels “which kept not their first estate” (Jud 6). Paul commands, “mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate” (Rom 12:16), and Psalm 136 blesses the God “who remembered us in our low estate” (Psa 136:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines estate as state; condition or circumstances of any person or thing; and rank; quality.
webster_full: ESTATE, n. In a general sense, fixedness; a fixed condition.
2. In a legal sense, the interest, or quantity of interest, a man has in lands, tenements, or other effects.
3. Condition or circumstances of any person or thing, whether high or low.
4. Rank; quality.
scriptures: For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.
And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.
Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever:
corruption_summary: Blessing is assumed to lift people out of low estate, and Mary's song says God regarded hers — the low estate was the address, not the obstacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 1:48 has a preposition worth pausing on: he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden. Not overlooked it, not removed it first — regarded it. Mary remained a poor young woman in an insignificant town; what changed was that God looked. The rest of the song generalizes it: he hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree; he hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.

Jude 6 uses estate the other way, of beings who left theirs: the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation. Discontent with an assigned station is presented as the archetypal fall, which sets Mary's response in sharp relief — behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. One party refused its estate; the other received it.
roots_summary: Greek tapeinosis (G5014), low estate, humiliation; arche (G746), beginning, first estate or principality; tapeinos (G5011), lowly.
roots_lines: Greek tapeinosis (G5014) — low estate, humiliation; Luke 1:48, Acts 8:33, James 1:10.
Greek arche (G746) — beginning, first estate; Jude 6.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — lowly, of low degree; Romans 12:16, Luke 1:52.
usage: “He hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden” — the address, not the obstacle.
“Kept not their first estate” — discontent with an assigned station.
“Who remembered us in our low estate” — the psalm's refrain of mercy.

pos: n. (a public showing; rendering Greek phanerosis and apokalupsis)
etymology: From Latin manifestus, caught in the act, evident. A manifestation is something made plain that was previously hidden.
biblical_def: A manifestation is a public showing. Paul explains spiritual gifts by it: “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” (1Co 12:7) — gifts are the Spirit becoming visible, and they are given for others. Romans speaks of creation waiting “for the manifestation of the sons of God” (Rom 8:19), and Paul commends the gospel by “manifestation of the truth” to every man's conscience (2Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines manifestation as the act of disclosing what is secret, unseen or obscure; discovery to the eye or to the understanding; and exhibition, display.
webster_full: MANIFESTATION, n. The act of disclosing what is secret, unseen, or obscure; discovery to the eye or to the understanding; the exhibition of any thing by clear evidence; display.
scriptures: But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
corruption_summary: Spiritual gifts are treated as personal endowments and ranked accordingly, and Paul defines them as the Spirit made visible, given to profit somebody else.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 12:7 settles two disputes at once: the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. Every man — so no believer is giftless. To profit withal — so no gift is for its holder. A congregation arguing about which gifts are greatest has already missed the definition; a manifestation is the Spirit showing Himself through a member for the benefit of the body, which makes comparison as pointless as a hand envying an eye.

2 Corinthians 4:2 gives the method of ministry that follows: by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. Not by craftiness, not by handling the word deceitfully — by making truth plain and letting it land on the conscience. The preacher's job is exposure, not persuasion by technique, and the verdict is left with the hearer before God.
roots_summary: Greek phanerosis (G5321), a making visible; phaneroo (G5319), to manifest; apokalupsis (G602), an unveiling — the word in Romans 8:19.
roots_lines: Greek phanerosis (G5321) — manifestation; 1 Corinthians 12:7, 2 Corinthians 4:2.
Greek apokalupsis (G602) — revelation, unveiling; Romans 8:19, the manifestation of the sons of God.
Greek phaneroo (G5319) — to make manifest; 1 John 3:2, when he shall appear.
usage: “The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” — no one giftless, no gift private.
“By manifestation of the truth” — exposure rather than technique.
“Waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God” — the unveiling creation expects.
